articles.excerpt: Introduction: security is no longer "the specialists' job" If you build web applications, scenes like these are probably becoming familiar: You wrote the login flow and the admin pages yourself. But s…
articles.body: Introduction: security is no longer "the specialists' job" If you build web applications, scenes like these are probably becoming familiar: You wrote the login flow and the admin pages yourself. But security checks keep slipping, because "there's nobody here who really knows that stuff." You let AI write more of your code now. Working software arrives faster, but you have no way to judge whether that code is safe. You promote AI adoption or digitalization inside your company, and when someone asks "is the security OK?", you are not sure what "OK" would even be based on. Few organizations have a dedicated security person. Yet when an incident happens, the people who respond are the ones who built the system or promoted it.

articles.title: Collaboration, Context, and Generated Assets: An Architecture Review of GenAnywhere, PlaceMaker, CityWeft, HalfMaps, and Tripo3D
articles.excerpt: Site modeling tools are usually evaluated as geometry engines. In practice, most of their cost and risk lives in a different layer: collaboration state. Where does the model live, who can change it, h…
articles.body: Site modeling tools are usually evaluated as geometry engines. In practice, most of their cost and risk lives in a different layer: collaboration state. Where does the model live, who can change it, how are conflicts reconciled, and what does each participant believe they are looking at? This review reads five tools — HalfMaps , PlaceMaker , CityWeft , GenAnywhere , Tripo3D — as collaboration architectures. HalfMaps: Read-Shared State Architecture: a browser client streaming tiled elevation and imagery from managed services, with a shallow local cache. Collaboration model: read-shared. Everyone sees the same service state; nobody edits the source. Implication: coordination cost near zero, and consistency guaranteed trivially — because nothing is authored.

articles.body: This post is part of the Monthly MLH × DEV Writing Challenge — a look back at what I built, how I built it, and what I'd do differently. This post is part of the Monthly MLH × DEV Writing Challenge — a look back at what I built, how I built it, and what I'd do differently.* The problem nobody asked me to solve I grew up around pomelo orchards in Meizhou, Guangdong. Every year, growers there make the same high-stakes guesses: which blocks are underperforming, where to fertilize, whether the irrigation is actually reaching the trees. Satellite data could answer all of this — Sentinel-2 flies over every five days, free for anyone to use. But "free data" and "usable answers" are very different things. No grower I know is going to open Google Earth Engine and write JavaScript.

articles.title: How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom
articles.excerpt: Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of our grid. The devices help efficiently move power across long distances, but they’re complicated and in short supply. And given that their basic…
articles.body: Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of our grid. The devices help efficiently move power across long distances, but they’re complicated and in short supply. And given that their basic design hasn’t changed much for about a century, they could use an upgrade.  As the world races to meet rising electricity demand from EVs, data centers, and more, researchers and companies are looking to modernize transformers. New, solid-state versions could help relieve some of the supply concerns and make sure the grid can handle the growing pressure. Conventional transformers generally rely on huge amounts of specialized steel alloys and miles of copper wire to do their work of transferring electricity between circuits.

articles.title: Your Android phone may remember AI chats you thought you deleted
articles.excerpt: Keeping your AI conversations offline doesn't necessarily mean they're gone when you delete them.
articles.body: TL;DR Tech researchers have developed a forensic tool that recovers deleted conversations from AI apps running locally on Android devices. In one experiment, the tool recovered 26 previously shared facts, compared with just 14 accessible to the original AI session. The technique requires forensic access to device data and doesn’t establish that conversations from cloud-based chatbots are similarly recoverable. Recovering deleted information from phones is hardly a new trick. We’ve seen it with text messages , photos, and other supposedly erased data. But researchers have taken things somewhere more intriguing: they’ve developed a forensic tool that can retrieve deleted AI conversations and actually bring the chatbot back to life, complete with some of its previous knowledge.

Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Noctilucent Clouds over Sweden Explanation: Sometimes it’s night on the ground but day in the air. As the Earth rotates to eclipse the Sun, sunset rises up from the ground. Therefore, at sunset on the ground, sunlight still shines on clouds above. Under usual circumstances , a pretty sunset might be visible, but unusual noctilucent clouds float so high up they can be seen well after dark.

articles.title: Analog astronauts: How living underwater can prepare humans for space missions
articles.excerpt: How living underwater can prepare humans for space missions
articles.body: I have been dreaming of doing research in space as an astronaut my whole life, but for some reason, the thought of working underwater made me nervous. I’ve known for a long time that astronauts train underwater to simulate different scenarios they’re likely to experience in space. Diving was never an issue for me, either — I even made it as far as becoming a certified rescue diver. So what was the problem? This summer, I led a simulated space mission in an underwater habitat called the Jules’ Undersea Lab. It is a research station that is located 22 feet (6.7 meters) underwater near Key Largo, Florida. You have to scuba dive to get in and out of the station. To become an aquanaut , you have to stay underwater for at least 24 hours in a so-called state of saturation.
